summary:
**MARS LANTERN: Martian Survival Atlas**

MARS LANTERN is a web-based field atlas that helps future astronauts plan and survive a journey across Mars. We developed an interactive, bounded map built on NASA Mars Trek imagery (Viking color mosaic, MOLA elevation and shaded relief). Users can type a place name or coordinates and instantly receive a Location Report covering terrain quality, a modeled temperature range, nearby water-ice, clay, sulfate, and iron-rich mineral resources, known hazards, and candidate routes. A Mission Builder lets them chain locations, choose objectives such as ice sampling or geology traverses, and test feasibility against terrain, resources, and daylight. A Mars Sky module computes sun position, seasons, Phobos, Deimos, and Earth for any site and time using Mars24 methods.

It addresses the challenge by turning scattered NASA datasets (MOLA, SWIM ice mapping, MEDA temperatures, rover traverses, CRISM mineralogy) into one practical survival guide. Every number carries a provenance badge (measured, NASA-derived, modeled, simulated, or unknown), and unknown terrain is never shown as safe.

This matters because the biggest risks on Mars are decisions made with unclear data. MARS LANTERN makes the evidence, its limits, and its uncertainty visible, so crews and planners can choose safer destinations and routes. It runs on GitHub Pages and exposes its science core through an MCP server for AI-assisted planning.
details:
MARS LANTERN: Project Details

What it does and how it works

MARS LANTERN is a static, bounded equirectangular Mars atlas with several connected modules:

  • Mars Map. A Leaflet map using an equirectangular coordinate system (EPSG:4326) with no world-wrapping, so the planet does not repeat endlessly. Base layers come from NASA Mars Trek (Viking color mosaic, MOLA shaded relief and elevation). Tile URLs are read from each product's WMTS GetCapabilities at build time rather than hard-coded. If Trek is unavailable, a cached global basemap takes over.
  • Checkpoint catalog. More than 40 typed sites: landing sites, water-ice zones (SWIM regions, polar deposits), mineral sites (clays, sulfates, hematite, carbonates, basaltic regolith, meteorite metal), and hazards. Coordinates from NASA sources and project documents are tagged with how they were verified.
  • Location Report. Users type a name or coordinates (several formats and both longitude conventions) or click the map. The report gives elevation and slope from a MOLA-derived DEM, a transparent terrain quality score, a modeled temperature range, resources within an adjustable radius, nearby hazards, candidate routes, a sky snapshot, and NASA imagery.
  • Mission Builder. Users chain locations, pick objectives (ice sampling, mineral survey, regolith collection, sensor deployment), choose vehicle and crew, and get A* routes. Separate verdicts for resources, terrain, schedule and daylight, and data coverage roll up into an overall result that is never better than its worst component. Missions export as JSON, Markdown, or PDF and are shareable by link.
  • Satellite view. Layer switching, a zoom-to-site mini map, a layer comparison slider, and live NASA Image and Video Library results.
  • Mars Sky. Sun position, local solar time, season (Ls), Mars Year, sunrise and sunset, Phobos, Deimos, and Earth's position, computed with the NASA Mars24 algorithm, with NASA Eyes on the Solar System embedded for context.
  • Provenance system. Every number is labeled MEASURED, NASA-DERIVED, MODELED, SIMULATED, or UNKNOWN. Missing data is never displayed as safe, and the router treats unknown terrain as impassable by default.

Benefits

  • Trustworthy. Users see where each value comes from and how uncertain it is.
  • Practical. One place answers "what is here, how hard is it to cross, how cold is it, where is the nearest ice, and when is there daylight?"
  • Resilient. A live, then cache, then fixture data strategy plus an offline mode keeps it running without internet.
  • Accessible. It is free and open source, runs in any browser, supports keyboard use and reduced motion, and works on small screens.
  • Honest. Known limits are stated openly: 463 m terrain data cannot resolve rocks or small scarps, temperature is a low-confidence estimate, and SWIM zones show likelihood, not confirmed ice.

Intended impact

The project aims to help mission planners, students, and the public understand that surviving on Mars depends on location: access to water, safe terrain, temperature, and daylight. It encourages evidence-based decisions by showing data limits alongside the data. It also corrects common misconceptions, for example by treating recurring slope lineae as a contested water signal and not as a water resource. Because the science logic is open and testable, others can reuse and extend it.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Languages: TypeScript (strict), Python (DEM processing), HTML and CSS.
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet with marker clustering, Recharts, React Router (HashRouter).
  • Science and data: Zod for schema validation, Fuse.js for search, astronomy-engine for planetary positions, Web Workers for routing, rasterio for DEM conversion.
  • NASA and partner data: Mars Trek WMTS, USGS Astrogeology mosaics, MGS MOLA DEM, SWIM ice mapping, Perseverance MEDA temperatures, CRISM and rover mineralogy, PDS rover tracks, NASA Image and Video Library, APOD, Mars24 ephemeris, NASA Eyes on the Solar System.
  • Infrastructure: Vitest, GitHub Actions (deploy and weekly data refresh), GitHub Pages, and a Model Context Protocol server built with the MCP SDK.
  • Development tools: AI-assisted development in Antigravity IDE, disclosed in docs/AI_USE.md. No special hardware is required; it runs on any modern browser.

Creativity

  • Lantern idea. The "carry the light, read the planet" concept frames the app as a field companion, not a data dump.
  • Evidence-first design. Provenance badges, score breakdown bars, and "unknown is never safe" make uncertainty visible, which is rare in map tools.
  • Location to mission in one flow. A user can type "Arcadia Planitia," see its ice likelihood, add an ice objective, route to it, check the daylight window with the sky module, and receive a feasibility verdict and share link.
  • Shared science core. The same tested code powers the website and an MCP server, so AI assistants can query Mars data and receive provenance-labeled answers.
  • Static but dynamic. Scheduled GitHub Actions refresh data and live NASA calls fall back gracefully, so a static site still behaves dynamically.

Factors considered

  • Data integrity. No fabricated values; sources are tagged, links are audited at build time, and uncertain coordinates are flagged for verification against NASA pages.
  • Coordinate conventions. East-positive 0 to 360° versus ±180° longitude, with calibration tests at Olympus Mons, Jezero, and Gale.
  • Scientific accuracy. Contested findings are labeled (RSL water status), and the temperature model is anchored to a published NASA range and marked low confidence.
  • Reliability. Offline mode, fallback basemap, and the live, cache, then fixture strategy keep demos from failing.
  • Performance. Lazy-loaded pages, compressed DEM data, and on-demand regional windows keep load times reasonable.
  • Safety and conservatism. Hard slope limits, terrain scoring with visible weights, and conservative verdicts that never exceed the worst component.
  • Accessibility and usability. Color-independent status cues, 44 px touch targets, and layouts that work down to 360 px.
  • Openness and ethics. Apache-2.0 license, NASA credit lines on all imagery, and clear disclosure of AI-assisted development.
  • Known limitations. Survival figures are simulation assumptions, not validated astronaut requirements, and the app states this plainly.
